The test image shows a split soybean stem/root held in hand. Key observations:
- Internal pith appears bleached white to light gray
- Outer stem surface is gray-brown with possible dark specks
- Plant is clearly dead/dry (harvested field background)
- Stem split lengthwise showing fibrous internal tissue

This is a **stem** specimen. Top candidates: White Mold (bleached white stems + sclerotia), Charcoal Rot (gray + microsclerotia), Sudden Death Syndrome (white pith when split).

Let me view one reference from each top candidate.

The White Mold references show black sclerotia externally. The Charcoal Rot reference shows a similar grayish external stem. Let me use my final reference view on Charcoal Rot's whole plant to compare internal pith color.

This final Charcoal Rot reference is very revealing. It shows a split stem with **white interior pith** and a grayish-dark exterior covered in tiny black microsclerotia — a near-identical match to the test image.

**Analysis summary:**
- Test image: split stem held in hand, white/bleached interior pith, grayish-tan exterior surface, dead/dry plant
- Charcoal Rot reference (Soybean_Dise_49.jpg): split stem showing white pith, exterior with characteristic dense tiny black speck pattern (microsclerotia) giving gray appearance
- White Mold would show larger, more obvious black sclerotia (rodent-dropping size) on/inside stem — not seen in test image
- SDS has white pith but the stem exterior wouldn't have the charcoal-gray microsclerotia appearance
- The grayish exterior surface in the test image matches the microsclerotia-laden Charcoal Rot stem
